content.content:
## 3. What microGPT needs from arrays

The vocabulary is `explorations/run-c4/src/FlatArrays.fsi`, inventoried in `reviews/c4-flatarrays-review.md` §1 at the committed version `a92569f83`: 38 declarations, of which 5 are aliases of library calls, 26 are new operations over the library's own array types, and 9 are new structures. (The working copy is under uncommitted repair after that review; Pavol's position of 2026-09-19 is that the model's operators stay operators and the vocabulary is repaired around the notation, `POSITIONS.md:38`, so the 26 stay operators and the compile path's overloading check must let them stand beside the prelude's `+`, `MAX` and juxtaposition, which is unmeasured.)

The 26 operations, by what they do to the data. Elementwise maps, 14: `+` and `-` with a scalar in both orders (4), the elementwise product `×`, `/` array by array and array by scalar (2), `MAX` with a scalar (2), `>` giving 0/1, `SQRT`, `exp`, `log`, and the broadcast add of a matrix to every plane of a rank-3 array (review rows 5-17 and 30). Contractions, meaning sums of products such as a matrix product, 2: the row scaling `diag(v) m` (row 20) and the plane-wise batched product of two rank-3 arrays (row 29); the 16×16 matrix product itself and `DOT` are the shipped library's own (`FortressLibrary.fss:2621-2629`) and are what the kernels time. Structural, 10: the row lift `rows(f, m)` in four shapes (31-34), `gather`, `onehot`, `pick`, `flat` (35-38) and the two transposes `^T` (39-40). The 9 structures are views: `Diag`, the transposed rank-3 array, the matrix over a slice of the flat parameter vector (`PView`), the row and plane-row views, and `heads`/`unheads`/`plane`, each a six-line object whose `get`/`put` index another array (review §1, last paragraph).

Element types needed: `RR64` for every weight and activation, `ZZ32` for keys and the integer corpus, `Char`/`String` for the corpus text in `FlatData`. Sizes: the hyperparameters are literals bound to names (`MicroGptFlat.fss:17`: 16, 16, 4, 4, 27, 26); the flat parameter vector's 4192 is computed; every constructor takes a run-time size and returns the unsized `Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]` or `Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\]` (`FlatArrays.fss:14-17` at `a92569f83`); nat-typed values enter through views built with `reflect` (`PView[\nat s, nat r, nat c\]`, `viewN(…, reflect(nr), reflect(nc))`, `:54-62`) and through the model's `Matrix`/`Array3` declarations: 20 of the api's declarations carry a nat, 25 in the focused base's `FlatArrays2.fsi`.

The measured cost of boxing on these shapes (`perf-probes/kernels/REPORT.md` §2; Java models of the runtime's own box, `Box[]` storage, against `double[]`): the 4192-element dot product 6.26× slower boxed, the 16×16 matrix product 6.53×, the row lift with `rmsn` 2.59×. The generic array object on top (an `Object[]` behind an interface with a `checkcast` per read) adds 9 %, 1.6 % and 4.8 %. The cost is the element boxes, not the container's genericity. None of the three kernels compiles today: 77 errors, `Array`, `Vector`, `Array3` undefined, all raised inside `FlatArrays.fsi`. All eighteen components of the two microGPT programs stop at disambiguation on `Array` (8), `Char` (5), `ImmutableArray` (3), `Vector` (2) (`compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19/microgpt-phase.md`); on the ladder, 42 files stop first on an array name (`ImmutableArray` 26, `Array1` 6, `Array` 6, `Array2` 2, the factory `array` 2; counted from `baseline-2026-09-19/ladder.tsv`).

## 4. The options as they stood before the rulings

Option (a), the interpreter's protocol ported boxed, is closed by Pavol's first ruling (§6) and is kept here only so the record shows what was rejected: about 1,200 lines of trait layer moved into `CompilerLibrary` over an `Object[]` native class; the fastest route to "the kernels compile"; the 6.3-6.5× kept; unboxing afterwards a second storage class under the same traits, "the same library written twice" (`map/README.md:127`).

### (b) `double[]`-backed arrays with unboxed elements designed in

What is built: `FRR64Vector.java` beside `FZZ32Vector.java`, the same 83 lines with `double[] val` and the four shape integers; `simpleDoubleVector.java` beside `simpleIntVector.java`; a trait in `CompilerBuiltin.fsi` with the nine members of `ZZ32Vector`; one line in `NamingCzar`'s special table and one in its foreign-route chain; a factory. That is the team's own five wiring sites. `ZZ32Vector` already covers the integer keys; `StringVector` the corpus.

Its own class, not a stamped instance: §2 verified that stamping substitutes class names into reference descriptors, so no instantiation of a generic template can hold a `double[]`; the `RR64` store is a hand-written class, as `FZZ32Vector` is, and anything reached through a generic trait's `get` is boxed at that boundary.

What the code generator must learn, if the loops are to run unboxed in generated code: an element read must become `getfield val:[D`, `iload i`, `daload` instead of the four-call chain of §2, and a bare `double` must have somewhere to go, which means a local variable slot of descriptor `D` and `dadd`/`dmul` for `RR64` arithmetic whenever the checker's static type is `RR64`, boxing only where a value meets a `T` or an `Any`. That is unboxing by static type (`performance-roadmap.md` A1) in `CodeGen.java` (6,750 lines) and `VarCodeGen`; every rung of it is a `.java` rung under the full gate with the 85 files as the net. Without it, an unboxed store with boxed traffic is what `ZZ32Vector` is today; whether that alone is faster than boxed storage is not measured, and the Java model that would answer it is one more class in `perf-probes/kernels/java/`.

A second route to unboxed loops needs no code-generator change: write the loops of the vocabulary's operations as Java natives over `double[]` (the dot product, the matrix product, the elementwise maps, `SQRT`/`exp`/`log` over an array), so a box is paid once per whole-array operation instead of once per element. This is the shape of an APL implementation, each primitive a native loop, and microGPT in the C4 form is whole-array vocabulary; the residue is the user lambdas passed to `fill`, `map` and `rows`, which box per element. Not the team's precedent: their `ZZ32Vector` operators are Fortress loops over boxed subscripts (`CompilerLibrary.fss:484-535`).

As first written, (b) carried sizes as run-time fields only and no nat in the type; Pavol's second ruling (§6) removes that half, so what survives of (b) is the store class and the two routes to unboxed loops, under the library's sized traits of §6.

### (c) The library's generic traits over per-element-type native stores

What is built: the interpreter's trait layer, `Indexed`, `ReadableArray`, `Array[\E,I\]`, `Array1[\T, nat b0, nat s0\]`, `Vector`, `Matrix`, `Array3`, with `fill`, `map`, `ivmap`, `t()` and the views written in Fortress as they are in `FortressLibrary.fss`; beneath them, in the place of `PrimitiveArray[\T, nat s0\]` (`__DefaultVector`'s `mem` field, `.fss:2204-2205`), one hand-written native store per element type: the `double[]` class of (b) for `RR64`, `FZZ32Vector` for `ZZ32`, a boxed `Object[]` store for every other `T`. The checker sees the library's own types; the model's `Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]`, `Vector[\RR64,s\]`, `Matrix[\RR64,r,c\]` resolve as written.

What selects the store. Not the checker: it has no notion of representation. The factory does, from the run-time type tag: a generic instantiation carries its arguments as run-time type descriptors (probe 1's `Box$RTTIc` holds a field `T` of type `RTTI`), so a native helper behind `array1[\T, nat s0\]()` can return the `double[]` store when `T`'s tag is `FRR64` and the boxed store otherwise, which is `performance-roadmap.md` A2's "class tag". Alternatively the vocabulary's `vec`/`mat` make the `RR64` store directly, which is what `FlatArrays.fss:14-17` already does through `array[\RR64\](n)`.

How a hand-written class sits under a stamped generic trait: `FZZ32Vector extends fortress.CompilerBuiltin.ZZ32Vector.DefaultTraitMethods implements ZZ32Vector` (`FZZ32Vector.java:16-17`), a non-generic Fortress trait whose generated abstract class the Java extends. So the store's trait must be non-generic (`RR64Store`), declared in Fortress as extending the generic `Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]`, and the generated abstract class then carries the stamped supertype. Unprobed: that a non-generic trait extending an instantiated generic supertype with a hand-written implementation class compiles and links; it is the first thing the array rung of §8 finds out.

Can Fortress's overloading express the specialisation? Not as two top-level declarations of one operator: `opr +[\I\](a: Array[\RR64,I\], s: RR64)` beside `opr +(a: RR64Store, s: RR64)` is one declaration with a static parameter and one without, forbidden by `Specification/basic/overloading.tex:100-105` and refused by the interpreter's check (the review's probe A). It is expressible as one declaration over the trait whose work is done by the object's own methods (`get`, `put`, `dot`, the product), which is the interpreter's own idiom for views (`TransposedMatrix`, `FortressLibrary.fss:2571-2588`) and ordinary virtual dispatch. Through the trait every `get` still boxes at the boundary; unboxed loops exist only inside the store's native methods (the second route of (b)) or after the code generator learns to unbox (the first route of (b)).

Cost: one `.java` rung (store class, factory helper, the non-generic store trait, full gate), one library rung (the trait layer in Fortress, `testFast` alone), then the native operations as in (b); all of it after or beside the nat rung of §6, because `Array1` and `Vector` cannot be declared before it. What it forecloses: nothing named; `ImmutableArray` (26 ladder files, through `List.fsi`) needs the immutable variant in every option.

## 5. What the specification and the team's own drafts say

The specification's array is a family of sized types over a generic one, and it keeps both factories. The type of a k-dimensional array expression is `Array k[T, 0, n0, …, 0, n_{k-1}]`, abbreviated `T[n0, …]`, with a footnote that "As of March 2008, the Fortress library provides Array k types for 1 ≤ k ≤ 3" (`Specification/basic/expressions/aggregate.tex:130-136`); a two-dimensional array of numbers "is a matrix", a one-dimensional one "is a vector", with the editors' margin notes reading "can be coerced to a matrix" (`:152-170`). The factory table gives `array[E](size)` for "the specified runtime-determined size" and `array1[E,n]()` for "statically determined size n" side by side (`advanced/parallelism-locality/arrays-distributed.tex:42-48`).

On storage: "As in Fortran, Fortress arrays are complex data structures; simple linear storage is encapsulated by the HeapSequence type, which is used in the implementation of arrays" (`arrays-distributed.tex:18-22`), with the note that distributions and `HeapSequence` "are not yet supported" (`:15-16`). Nothing in the prose says boxed or unboxed; the intent is an array as a structure over a linear store, which (c) is.

On sizes in types: "types can be parametric with respect to other types and values (most notably natural numbers)" (`preliminaries/intro/nutshell.tex:85-86`); the nat chapter is quoted in §6.

On the intended aggregate: "Guy's proposal for making tensors the principal user-level indexed aggregate type in Fortress (06/27/07)" and his email "Arrays, matrices, and tensors (short)" of 12/15/06 (`appendices/future.tex:63-65`); the FAQ's answer to variable-sized arrays with static bounds checking is a link to a wiki page that no longer exists (`appendices/FAQ.tex:55-57`); the emails themselves are not in the repository (`map/design-intent-sources.md:111, 128`).

On the compiled encoding: the JVM paper says "mentions of static parameters are replaced with their upper bounds in domain and range" (`Papers/Implementation/MethodMapping.tex:134`), which is why stamping is a renaming, and that the template's side file "contains info about the static parameters, including their names, whether they are types, oprs, or nats" (`:142`), which the tree does (§6). The team's own unboxing note is `compiler/optimization/Unbox.java:18-30`: four cases, "primitive. ZZ{8,16,32,64}, RR{32,64}, Boolean", singleton objects, unboxed fields, "comprises unboxed"; a taxonomy referenced by nothing.

The drafts say nothing about arrays. `Library/incomplete/` (24 files) contains no mention of an array. `Library/GeneratorLibrary.fss` and `.fsi` (783 lines, imported by nothing) are the generator and reduction protocol, `Container`, `DefaultGeneratorImplementation`, without `Indexed` or any array. `Fortress.Operators.fsi.INCOMPLETE` is the algebra above `Number` and names no aggregate. What the team shipped in this world is `ZZ32Vector`, and it is the only precedent with code behind it.

## 6. The nat plan: what the second fork must deliver for the first

Pavol's rulings of 2026-09-19, in his words. On boxing: "we must go to double array for performance. There is again no question about this. If this should have been high performance language, it cannot be boxed." On sizes: "I don't know [that] we can sidestep the nat issue. That is a central design point that they are using." So the sized types are built as the team designed them, `Vector[\T, nat s0\]` and `Matrix[\T, nat s0, nat s1\]`, the checker is taught nat parameters, and the two forks are taken together. On method: "study the existing parts of the Fortress library meticulously, and use those patterns for extending the standard library in the native way"; microGPT's operations go into the standard library in its spirit, not into a user file.
## 7. The decision tree, with two questions closed

Question 1, boxed or `double[]`: closed by Pavol, `double[]`. Consequence: the `RR64` store is a hand-written class on the `FZZ32Vector` pattern, never a stamped generic (§2), and the boxed `Object[]` store exists only for element types that have no native store.

Question 4, where sizes live: closed by Pavol, in the type as the team designed. Consequences: the checker rung of §6e precedes the first sized declaration; the export checker and the object crash are on the path, not optional; every distinct size is a stamped class; the run-time-sized factory returns the unsized `Array` until the string-from-number route is probed (§6d, default).

Question 2, open: what implements the library's sized traits under `double[]`?
Branch "native stores per element type under the library's generic objects": `__DefaultVector[\T, nat s0\]` keeps its shape and its `mem` field is the `RR64` store for `RR64`, `FZZ32Vector` for `ZZ32`, the boxed store otherwise, chosen by the factory from the run-time type tag; the interpreter's own layering with `PrimitiveArray` replaced; one unprobed link, the non-generic store trait under the generic `Array` (§4c).
Branch "the loader picks a `double[]` template per instantiation": the expando route; `PrimitiveArray⟦FRR64,4192⟧` would load a different class than `PrimitiveArray⟦FZZ32,4192⟧`; nothing of it exists, and the instantiater's only tool is name substitution.
Default: the first; it needs one probe and no loader change, and it is the library's own structure.

Question 3, open: where do the loops run unboxed?
Branch "inside native whole-array operations": Java helpers over `double[]` for the contractions and elementwise maps; a box per operation; no code-generator change; the user lambdas of `fill`, `map`, `rows` still box per element.
Branch "in generated code": the code generator learns `D` locals, `daload`/`dastore`, `dadd`/`dmul` for statically `RR64` code; every rung `.java` under the full gate; unlocks unboxed loops written in Fortress.
Default: natives first, with the kernel measurement in the first array rung; generated-code unboxing as PLAN's step 4, once the measured residue says what it is worth.

Question 5, open, from the third ruling: the library's unused nats (`.fsi:1496-1523`). Branch "default an unconstrained nat to `0`" keeps the library's text; branch "refuse and delete the dead parameters" edits six library declarations. Default: the first, the plan's own recommendation, and the only reason the checker rung would otherwise touch `Library/`.

Where microGPT's 26 operations go is not a question after the third ruling: into `CompilerLibrary` in the library's own style, whose precedent for scalar extension is the `ZZ32` block at `FortressLibrary.fss:4477-4517` (`opr +(x: Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\], y: ZZ32)` beside `AdditiveGroup.+`, the same overloading shape the review found illegal by the letter and the interpreter accepts), for maps `map(f)` over `replica`, for structure the view objects, and for products the shared-nat operators of §6c.

## 8. What happens right after the choice

First, the checker rung (`.scala`, full gate): the four tests of §6e, the shadow session for the two unknowns, then the edit of `nat-checking-plan.md` §f with option A. What it moves: no ladder file by itself (the plan's census), no microGPT component; it unblocks every sized declaration.

Second, the array rung (`.java`, full gate), the first failing test `library_tests/Vector1.fss`: `v = vector[\RR64,3\](fn (i: ZZ32): RR64 => 1.5 i); if v[1] + v[2] = 4.5 then println("PASS") end`, failing today at disambiguation on `Vector`; then the `RR64` store class and helper, the non-generic store trait under `Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]` (the probe of §4c first), `Indexed`, `ReadableArray`, `Array`, `Array1`, `Vector` and `__DefaultVector` in the library's spelling, the factories; in the same rung `kdot` compiled over a native `dot` and timed against `KDotPrim`. What it moves: the ladder's `Array` 6, `array` 2 and `Array1` 6 past disambiguation; of the eighteen microGPT components, the 8 stopped on `Array` and the 2 on `Vector` reach the checker.

Third, library-only rungs: `Array2`, `Matrix`, the transposed views and the shared-nat products (`kmat` timed); `Array3`; the scalar extension and elementwise maps for `RR64` arrays in the `ZZ32` block's style, which is where the compile path's overloading check on the model's operator pairs is measured; `Char` (5 components) and the immutable variant (`ImmutableArray`, 3 components and 26 ladder files) in whichever order the counts rank them.

## 9. The probes behind §2 and §6 (2026-09-19, private cache, nothing committed)

The compiler world's library was compiled into a private `FORTRESS_CACHES` in the order of `repo-internals.md:170-179` (five components, all exit 0), and each probe was `fortress compile` then `fortress run` from the scratchpad.

Probe 1, stamping. `object Box[\T\](x: T) getter get(): T = x end` with `Box[\RR64\](1.5)` and `Box[\ZZ32\](3)`; prints `4.0` and `4`. The jar holds the template `GenBox$Box⟦⟧.class`, whose `javap -p` shows `Field "\%x":LT;` and `public T get()`. Run with `-Dfortress.bytecodes.expanded.directory` set, the loader saved the stamped `GenBox$Box⟦…FRR64⟧.class`, whose field is `Lcom/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FRR64;` and whose `get` returns `FRR64`. A reference descriptor before and after; the stamped class's `RTTIc` carries a field `T` of type `RTTI`.

Probe 2, element traffic on the unboxed vector. `v = makeZZ32Vector(4); v[0] := 3; x = v[0] + 1; println(x)`; prints `4`. `javap -c` of the program: `invokevirtual FZZ32Vector."[]"(FZZ32)FZZ32` then `checkcast FZZ32`; of `CompilerBuiltin$ZZ32Vector$DefaultTraitMethods.getValue`: `invokestatic native/…/simpleIntVector.getIndexedValue(FZZ32Vector, FZZ32)FZZ32`; of that generated wrapper in `nativewrapper_cache`: `FZZ32.getValue()I`, `simpleIntVector.getIndexedValue(FZZ32Vector, I)I`, `FZZ32.make(I)`.

Probe 3, an explicit nat used in no type. `f[\nat n\](x: ZZ32): ZZ32 = x + 1` called as `f[\3\](1)` compiles and prints `2`.

Probe 4, a nat object. `object Vec[\nat n\](v: ZZ32Vector) getter len(): ZZ32 = |v| end` with `Vec[\4\](makeZZ32Vector(4))` fails in the checker, rc 1, no class written: `java.lang.ClassCastException: class com.sun.fortress.nodes.VarType cannot be cast to class com.sun.fortress.nodes.IntExpr`, frames `NodeUpdateVisitor.forIntArg` ← `StaticTypeReplacer.replaceIn:102` ← `STypesUtil.relativizer:1542` ← `gatherMethods:1548`. The same with `extends Sized[\n\]` added, and with `getter size(): ZZ32 = n` added.

Probe 5, a nat needing inference. The object of probe 4 with `same[\nat n\](a: Vec[\n\], b: Vec[\n\]): ZZ32 = a.len + b.len` and `same(x, y)`: `java.lang.Error: Not yet implemented`, rc 1.

Probe 6, a nat in value position. `foo[\nat n\](): ZZ32 = n.asZZ32 + 1` with `println(foo[\5\]())` and `println(foo[\4192\]())` compiles; the caller's bytecode names `foo⟦5⟧` and `foo⟦4192⟧`; the template body reads `getstatic NatVal$n.ONLY:Lfortress/CompilerBuiltin$IntLiteral;`; the run dies with `NoClassDefFoundError: NatVal$n`. The side file `NatVal⚙$foo⟦⟧….xlation` reads `function 1 6 intnat 1 n`.

3:# Review of the array design for the compiled world
5:## 0. What was checked and how
11:## 1. Findings
13:### Decisive 1. The design keeps the model's unsized static types and never checks the model's applications against a static checker; as written, nothing in microGPT and none of the three kernels passes the type checker, whatever the storage is
27:### Decisive 2. The default for "what implements the sized traits over the store" has no checked mechanism on this path; the checker refuses it, including through the library's own selection idiom
37:### Decisive 3. The second reserved fork, the library route, is closed by default in §7, against the ruling as it was applied the same evening
47:### Serious 4. "Natives first" contradicts the ruling's letter, has no team precedent, and is measured to deliver nothing on the shapes the model is made of
57:### Serious 5. The census "no arithmetic occurs inside white brackets anywhere in the library" is false for the three storing objects the array rungs need
65:### Serious 6. The array rung of §8 hides three pieces of `.java` work, so the count of gated batches is at least three, not two
75:### Serious 7. The unconstrained-nat default is unsafe and does not address what the export checker will actually meet
83:### Serious 8. The design gives no stop condition, and the ones `PLAN.md` has do not cover the failures this plan can meet
87:### Minor 9. The "unprobed link" of §4c is already proven by the tree, and the rung's first experiment is misdirected
91:### Minor 10. "The one recorded implementation stance" is a conditional inside a question
95:### Minor 11. What the specification's own breadcrumb on unboxed arrays says, which the design does not cite
99:### Minor 12. Two numbers in §3 are the review's, not the tree's
103:## 1b. The design's nat rungs against `reviews/nat-checking-plan.md`
115:## 2. The seven questions, answered by finding
131:## 3. Decisions that are Pavol's
135:### Decision A. What puts `double[]` under the library's sized traits
145:### Decision B. Where loops run unboxed
155:### Decision C. Which library the array layer and the model's operations go into
165:### Decision D. The model's static types
175:### Decision E. The six api declarations with dead nats
185:### Decision F. What the first gated rung is, and what stops the climb
191:## 4. Verdict
=== §3 ===
## 3. Decisions that are Pavol's

Each as what we do, what it changes, the alternatives, and a labelled default that can be accepted without reading the argument; the argument is in §1.

### Decision A. What puts `double[]` under the library's sized traits

What we do: choose the mechanism by which `Vector[\RR64,16\]` gets a `double[]` store while `Vector[\T,16\]` for other `T` gets a boxed one.

What it changes: which `.java` rung the array work needs first, and whether the library's generic factories keep their text.

Alternatives. (A1) The design's default, a factory selecting by run-time type tag under one generic storing object: refused by the checker (finding 2); to keep it, a code-generator special case for the factory, a `.java` rung with no team precedent. (A2) The team's direction: the code generator and loader give a stamped `PrimitiveArray⟦FRR64,n⟧` a `double[]` field, `Unbox.java` case 1 plus the expando stub; the library's text stays as it is; the largest change, in the loader and `CodeGen`, and `PLAN.md` step 5's own first probe. (A3) Monomorphic storing objects per native element type (`__RR64Vector[\nat s0\]`) beside the generic boxed one, with a monomorphic factory name per element type in the manner of `array1`/`vector` (`.fss:2251`); typed cleanly, no code-generator change, but the model then names `rr64vector`, not `vector`, and the generic `Vector[\T,s0\]` is boxed for every `T` including `RR64` unless the user calls the right factory.

Default: probe A2 first (one shadow experiment, `next-climb.md` §3b's first item), because it is the team's breadcrumb and `PLAN.md`'s order; A3 is the fallback that needs no `.java`; A1 is closed by the probe unless Pavol wants the special case.

### Decision B. Where loops run unboxed

What we do: choose between Java natives per whole-array operation and unboxing `RR64` by static type in generated code.

What it changes: whether the ruling "it cannot be boxed" holds for the model (views, lambdas, `rows`) or only for whole-array operations on stores; and the size of the code-generator work.

Alternatives. (B1) Natives first, the design's default: measured at 8.9×/6.6× primitive on the model's shapes (finding 4), the same as boxed storage; helps `p DOT p` and Adam only; no precedent. (B2) Unboxing by static type first (roadmap A1, `Unbox.java` case 1): `D` locals, `daload`/`dastore`, `dadd`/`dmul` wherever the checker's type is `RR64`; the library's own Fortress loops (`fill`, `map`, `Vector.dot`) become unboxed without natives; every rung `.java` under the full gate; the team's precedent. (B3) Both, in the order B2 for element access and arithmetic, natives only where a whole-array kernel beats the JIT (a measured residue, not a default).

Default: B2, because it is the only alternative under which the ruling is true of the model, and the kernel measurement in the array rung is then `kdot` in Fortress against `KDotPrim`, not against a native.

### Decision C. Which library the array layer and the model's operations go into

What we do: choose between growing the compiler world (`CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin`, `CompilerAlgebra`) with a copy of the array layer and the algebra above `Number`, and making the interpreter's library (`FortressLibrary`) the prelude the compiler checks.

What it changes: whether the standard library exists once or twice from here on; whether yesterday's commit to `FortressLibrary.fss` and this design's rungs land in the same file; the 92 tower errors and 108 native bindings of the library route (FACTS) against the second copy of about 1,200 lines plus the algebra.

Alternatives. (C1) The compiler world, the design's default. (C2) The library route, `PLAN.md`'s reserved fork: the interpreter's library becomes the checked prelude; the 92 errors are classified first (`next-climb.md` §3b's last item, "one probe"). (C3) One text, two bindings: the array layer and algebra written once in `Library/` in Fortress, with the native bindings the only per-world file (`NativeArray.fss` with `builtinPrimitive` for the interpreter, a compiler-world twin with `import java`); whether the two worlds can share a prelude file is unprobed.

Default: none can be labelled; this is the reserved fork and it is Pavol's. The cheapest fact before deciding is the classification of the 92 errors.

### Decision D. The model's static types

What we do: decide how `MicroGptFlat.fss` and `FlatArrays.fss` are typed for a static checker, given that today their values are statically unsized and their operations are declared on sized types (finding 1).

What it changes: the model's text, or the vocabulary's declarations, or the compile path.

Alternatives. (D1) The model carries sizes in its types as the specification intends (`makeVector`, `trait-parameters.tex:94-97`): `step` and its helpers become generic in `nat` parameters, the hyperparameters become static arguments, and every `Array[\RR64,…\]` in the model becomes a `Vector`/`Matrix`/`Array3` with nats; the ruling of `POSITIONS.md:38` requires the diff to be shown before it is built. (D2) The vocabulary is declared over the unsized `Array[\RR64,I\]` and the products the model uses (`DOT`, juxtaposition, `rows`, `gather`, `diag`) are added over `Array` beside the library's sized ones; the model's text is unchanged; the sized products and the shape check are then not what the model exercises, which is the sidestep the second ruling refuses. (D3) A compile-path `reflect`: a native that asks the loader for `N⟦n⟧` by name at run time, which the team's own comment asks for ("we ought to build it in", `NatReflect.fss:39`); it keeps the model's dynamic dispatch but does not make the static types sized, so it does not by itself pass the checker; it is what D1 needs for the run-time-sized parameter vector.

Default: D1 with D3, because both rulings are honoured only there; D2 is the honest alternative if the model's text is to stay byte-identical. The first thing to show Pavol is the D1 diff of `rmsn` and `step`'s signature, not a rung.

### Decision E. The six api declarations with dead nats

What we do: decide what the checker does with `nat m` and `nat p` in `.fsi:1496-1523`, which the component does not have.

What it changes: whether the checker rung touches `Library/` (six api lines) and what an unsolved nat means anywhere.

Alternatives. (E1) Default to 0, the design's: unsafe when the parameter is later used as a value (finding 7), and blind to the api/component shape mismatch. (E2) Unsolved is an error when the nat reaches a type, a name or a value, nothing otherwise (the interpreter's `BottomType` rule); the six declarations pass because their dead parameters reach nothing; the export checker compares by name and reports the extra parameter. (E3) Delete the dead parameters from the api, a sealed-tree library edit flagged at commit, and the export checker then agrees.

Default: E2 in the checker, E3 as the library edit shown to Pavol as a six-line diff; not E1.

### Decision F. What the first gated rung is, and what stops the climb

What we do: run a shadow rung with no gate before the checker rung, answering: where the `VarType`/`IntExpr` crash comes from; what the export checker reports on the six declarations; whether a generic object with a nat argument in `extends` can be stamped and run (`NatExtends1`); whether the store can be selected under the generic factory in any typed way (`NatStore1`, decision A); and whether the loader can be made to select a representation (decision A2). Then the checker rung.

Stop conditions to adopt, each returning to Pavol with the capture: the crash's fix is in a Java front-end class, so the plan's "no Java" and its size are void; a nat argument needs a new RTTI kind in `runtimeSystem/`; the checker refuses every typed route to the store (A1 and A3 both fail); the model cannot be typed without a diff to its lines (decision D not taken); the kernel compiled over the store lands at the `KDotStore` number rather than the `KDotPrim` number, which means the traffic is still boxed.

## 4. Verdict

### Decisive 3. The second reserved fork, the library route, is closed by default in §7, against the ruling as it was applied the same evening

What the design says. §7, last paragraph: "Where microGPT's 26 operations go is not a question after the third ruling: into `CompilerLibrary` in the library's own style"; §4c and §8: the interpreter's trait layer "written in Fortress as they are in `FortressLibrary.fss`" into the compiler world.

What the ruling said and did. `POSITIONS.md:39`: "all the extensions that [microGPT] invented need to go directly to the standard library in the spirit of the standard library." The commit that applied it, `02d09a39f` (`postmortem-2026-09-19/array-work-brief.md` §1), edited `Library/FortressLibrary.fss` and `.fsi`, the interpreter's library. `PLAN.md`, stop conditions: what stops the climb includes "the library route, the interpreter's library as prelude against growing the compiler library beyond what one rung needs". `next-climb.md` §3a: "the second reserved fork — the library route … is entangled with it".

What building in the compiler world means, which the design does not say. The compiler world has no `AdditiveGroup` and no `MultiplicativeRing` (`Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss:15-25` holds `Equality` and `StandardTotalOrder` only; the scalar-extension review says the same at `:162`), no `Indexed`, no `ReadableArray`, no `Array`; `Vector[\T extends Number, nat s0\] extends { AnyVector, Array1[\T,0,s0\], AdditiveGroup[\Vector[\T,s0\]\] } excludes { AnyMultiplicativeRing }` (`.fss:2191-2193`) cannot be declared "as the team designed" without the algebra above `Number` being written a second time in that world. From then on the standard library exists in two texts: the interpreter's, which the checker never sees, and the compiler's, which it does; the map's warning "the same library written twice" (`map/README.md:127`) was about boxed and unboxed, and it applies here unchanged. The design never mentions `comprises`, `excludes` validation, `AdditiveGroup`, `CompilerAlgebra`, or the 92 tower errors the checker raises on the interpreter's library (FACTS, the interpreter's library fed to the compiler), which are what the library route costs and what the compiler-world route avoids by copying.

Severity. A reserved fork decided in one line of a worker's document, which `POSITIONS.md:48` says is a decision not made. It goes to Pavol as decision C.

### Serious 4. "Natives first" contradicts the ruling's letter, has no team precedent, and is measured to deliver nothing on the shapes the model is made of

What the design says. §7 question 3, default: "natives first, with the kernel measurement in the first array rung; generated-code unboxing as PLAN's step 4"; §4b admits "Without it, an unboxed store with boxed traffic is what `ZZ32Vector` is today; whether that alone is faster than boxed storage is not measured".

Measured now (`compiler-probes/array-design-review/java-medians.tsv`, the kernels' harness, medians of 3). Unboxed `double[]` storage read and written through a boxing accessor, arithmetic boxed as the runtime boxes it: `kdot` 0.007559 s, 8.9× primitive, against boxed storage 0.005495 s (6.4×) and primitive 0.000852 s; `kmat` 0.005552 s, 6.6×, against boxed 0.005255 s (6.2×) and primitive 0.000844 s. The store buys nothing until the traffic is unboxed; the design's §2 already showed the traffic on `ZZ32Vector` is four calls and an allocation per element (probe 2).

Where the model's traffic is. The model's data design is views: nine `PView`s over the flat vector, `RowView`, `Row3View`, `heads`, `unheads`, `plane`, `Diag`, `Transposed3` (`FlatArrays.fss:40-120`), each a `get` that indexes another array. A native product over a view reads its operand through `get`, boxed; a native `dot` over the store helps `p DOT p` and Adam's three lines (`MicroGptFlat.fss:76-79`) and nothing in `step`. So the first rung's number (`kdot` over a store) would not transfer to the program the number is for.

Precedent. The team's compiler-world operators over `ZZ32Vector` are Fortress `for` loops over boxed subscripts (`CompilerLibrary.fss:484-535`), and the team's unboxing note is a code-generator taxonomy (`Unbox.java`); the design says of natives "Not the team's precedent" (§4b) and defaults to them anyway. The route with the precedent, and the only one under which "it cannot be boxed" is true of the model, is unboxing by static type in generated code (roadmap A1, `Unbox.java` case 1), which is the largest code-generator work in the plan. Decision B.

# Two libraries

Terms used below. **Prelude**: the set of apis the compiler implicitly imports into every component, so a program can name `ZZ32` without importing anything. **World**: a prelude plus the switches that go with it; `fortress <file>.fss` runs the interpreter's world, `fortress compile` the compiler's. **Rung**: one declaration added to a prelude with a failing test, gated on `ant testFast` and `ant testSystem`.

## 1. When the split was made, and in whose words

The compiler's prelude was born on **2008-12-19** in commit `c8d301411` by **Jan-Willem Maessen** (`jmaessen`), whose whole message is: *"[libraries, interpreter] Preliminary version of stripped-down minimalist fortress library for first crack at compilation, plus interpreter support to let it all run through gracefully."* It created `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss` (27 lines: two `print` bindings and an empty `trait String`), `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss` (49 lines), and the world switch itself, then in `interpreter/glue/WellKnownNames.java`.

The switch was documented as provisional in the same commit, in a comment that is still in the tree at `compiler/WellKnownNames.java:109-111`: *"Re-points fortressLibrary etc. to special compiler (rather than interpreter) versions of the code. **Hopefully temporary hack as we work on importing java objects cleanly.**"* Note the stated reason: importing Java objects. Not the type checker — the first `CompilerBuiltin` still bound its natives with `builtinPrimitive` and the interpreter's glue package; `import java` arrived three months later (`b2880c05c` 2009-03-03, *"We now import java.lang.Math, but we don't use it yet"*; `2f8744701` 2009-03-09).

Three further facts from the history. A **third** prelude existed for a month — `352c78880` (EricAllen, 2009-02-06) *"Added TypeCheckerLibrary and TypeCheckerBuiltin; threaded through front-end"*, removed by `904bd2684` (sukyoungryu, 2009-03-09) *"[type checker] Eliminated type checker libraries"*; its residue is `Types.useTypeCheckerLibraries()` (`compiler/Types.java:90-92`), which now just calls `useCompilerLibraries()`. The split's maintenance cost shows up early: `ce1366c17` (2010-02-25) *"Fixed a bug in Shell: use the interpreter library instead of the compiler library when running tests with the interpreter. (Found by Chulwoo Lee)"*. And the team had a word for what it was putting in the compiler's library: *"Tested by adding **bogus** Array traits in the CompilerLibrary. Tests should be added when generic traits can be compiled"* (`ccccbe26f`, 2009-10-04), *"It should use a parameterized Generator type but it is not yet supported. Instead, we use GeneratorZZ32 for now. Added **bogus** IN and = operators"* (`525264af1`, 2009-10-02), and, a month before the wind-down, David Chase's *"Added missing CMP method to **bogo-trait** ZZ32"* (`b16964470`, 2012-06-27). `compiler/Types.java:73-76` names the pair the way they thought of it: *"the compiler libraries"* against *"the full libraries"*.

**The specification knows one library, not two.** `Specification/library/structure.tex:13-22`: the automatically imported libraries are *"chiefly `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`"*; `library/default-libraries.tex:15-24`: *"Two sets of libraries are imported into every Fortress program by default"* — `FortressLibrary` and the builtins. `CompilerLibrary` appears in no `.tex` in the tree, and Sun's own `README.txt:432-437` says the same. The split is an implementation fact the published design never acknowledged.

**What no source says.** No commit message, no README, no text under `Papers/`, no spec `\note{}` states an intention to compile the full library one day, or any plan for ending the split. The record runs the other way: the compiler prelude was still being grown declaration by declaration in the project's last month. The wind-down note names the wall the project stopped at, and it is the same one — *"the mismatch between the (rather ambitious) Fortress type system and a virtual machine not designed to support it"* — while listing *"symmetric multiple inheritance with type exclusion"* among the eight things they were pleased with (`research/extracts/fortress-websites-wayback.md:110-123`). Exclusion is what two thirds of §3's errors are about.

## 2. What the two libraries share, and where they differ

**Sizes.** Compiler world: `CompilerLibrary.fss/.fsi` 718 + 358 lines, `CompilerBuiltin.fss/.fsi` 1,636 + 786 — 3,498 in all. Interpreter world: `FortressLibrary` 4,507 + 2,550, `FortressBuiltin` 701 + 218 — 7,976. `AnyType.fss` (17 lines) is shared. Since ladder rung 1 (`1bd8d3ad1`) the compiler prelude is four apis, not three: `compilerAlgebra()` is no longer commented out at `WellKnownNames.java:124`, which supersedes `map/dormant-code.md` §1.4. `Library/GeneratorLibrary` (469 + 314) remains unwired.

**Written twice.** Counting top-level declarations in the four api files by kind and name: 183 in the compiler world, 276 in the interpreter's, **75 in both** — 21 traits (`ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN64`, `RR64`, `ZZ`, `Number`, `String`, `Generator`, `Maybe`, `Range`, `Matrix`, `Comparison`, `TotalComparison`, `Reduction`, `Condition`, the exception roots), 27 objects, 9 operator names and 18 functions. The operator figure is by name and so under-reports: `opr` declaration lines alone number 346 in the compiler world's apis against 496 in the interpreter's. 108 declarations exist only in the compiler world, 63 of them the `characterXxx` category constants and the fixed-size integer bounds. **201 exist only in the interpreter's**: the array and range vocabulary (`Array`, `Array1..3`, `ImmutableArray`, `Vector`, `Indexed`, `Rank`, the `Range` family), the reductions and generators (`SumReduction`, `BigReduction`, `MonoidReduction`, `Comprehension`, `BigOperator`), the algebra above `Number` (`QQ`, `Integral`, `AnyIntegral`, `StandardTotalOrder`, `AdditiveGroup`, `MultiplicativeRing`, `LexicographicOrder`), `Thread`, and the factory and reflection functions (`array`, `matrix`, `vector`, `immutableArray`, `region`).

**The two native binding mechanisms.** The interpreter writes `builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.Int$Less")` as the body; the evaluator pattern-matches that literal call and substitutes the named Java class for the body (`glue/NativeApp.java:157-215`, reached only from `interpreter/evaluator/values/FunctionClosure.java:47-57`), and the class takes the evaluator's boxed `FValue`/`FObject` and returns `FBool.make(…)`. 339 such bindings in the two interpreter prelude files (108 in `FortressLibrary.fss`, 231 in `FortressBuiltin.fss`), 427 across the whole interpreter library. The compiler writes `import java com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.{simpleIntArith.intLT => jIntLT}` and then an ordinary call `jIntLT(self, other)`: 330 such aliases in 20 `import java` blocks, over 370 public static methods in 25 classes under `nativeHelpers/`.

**Could one text carry both?** Not in the `builtinPrimitive` direction: the name is declared only at `FortressBuiltin.fsi:30`, nothing under `compiler/` or `codegen/` refers to it, and a component that gives it a body compiles and then calls that body, the class-name string being inert data (`perf-probes/prelude/REPORT.md` §3, `07-builtinprimitive-probe.out`). The other direction is **not obviously blocked, and this is new here**: `ForeignJava`, which reads a Java class with ASM and synthesizes an api for it, lives in the shared `repository/` package and is wired into the *interpreter* as well as the compiler — `interpreter/Driver.java:441`, `interpreter/env/ForeignComponentWrapper.java:59`, `interpreter/env/ClosureMaker.java:64`. None of the 381 `.fss` files in `ProjectFortress/tests/`, the interpreter's own corpus, contains an `import java` line. So the mechanism is wired on both sides and exercised on one; whether an `import java` binding runs under the interpreter is one small probe that nobody has run.

**A difference that is not in the library files.** `Shell.useCompilerLibraries()` (`Shell.java:371-386`) flips three desugaring settings besides the prelude names, and one of them changes the language the text is written in: `setExtendsObjectPreDesugaring(true)` makes `PreDisambiguationDesugaringVisitor.forStaticParam` (`:134-148`) rewrite an unbounded static parameter's extends clause in the compiler world and leave it alone in the interpreter's. `Types.useCompilerLibraries()` (`compiler/Types.java:72-83`) additionally re-points `String`, `JavaString`, `Exception` and `CheckedException` from the library api to the builtin one. A shared text has to be correct under both settings, or the settings have to be reconciled first.

## 3. The errors, classified

Re-measured for this brief rather than taken from the record: the probe's own driver (`perf-probes/prelude/WorldFlip.java` with its instrumented `StaticChecker` copy) re-run on the tree at `29a827877` under a private cache (`-Dfortress.caches`, honoured through `ProjectProperties.java:261-269,283`); `default_repository/` was not touched. Result: **93 errors at 96 locations across 48 declaration sites**, not the 92 on record. The extra one is the revival's own: commit `02d09a39f` (2026-09-19) gave `AnyIntegral` a `comprises { ZZ }` clause, and the checker now applies the comprises rule to `Integral[\I\] extends { …, AnyIntegral }` at `FortressLibrary.fsi:411`. Everything else is the same set shifted by three lines. The crash that follows is unchanged (`Not yet implemented`, `STypesUtil.scala:557`).

| family | errors | sites | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| A `Type X excludes Y but it extends Y` | 36 | — | see below |
| B `Types A and B exclude each other. C must not extend them` | 26 | 27 (A and B together) | see below |
| C `Ill-formed type` + `static argument I does not satisfy the bound Integral[\I\]` | 26 | 15 | library defect |
| D `multiple declarations of split / splitWithOffsets with the same parameter type: ()` | 2 | 2 (+2 secondary) | library defect |
| E `Invalid comprises clause: … should not be extended` | 2 | 2 | library against a rule the spec states only in a note |
| F return type not a subtype of the overridden one | 1 | 1 (+1 secondary) | library defect |

**A and B are one phenomenon under two message templates, and they are not one verdict.** The checker builds its exclusion relation from four clauses (`scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala:423-457`): an explicit `excludes` clause (`checkEC`), a `comprises` clause (`checkCC`), object-ness (`checkO`), and **two distinct instantiations of the same generic ancestor** (`checkP`). Only the first is in the specification, which derives exclusion from `excludes` clauses and symmetry alone (`Specification/basic/traits.tex:218-228`). Of the 27 sites: **one** is a defect on anybody's reading — `FortressLibrary.fsi:2526` extends and excludes `Condition[\()\]` in the same declaration, which the spec's own *"neither can extend the other"* forbids; **two declarations across five lines** (`SumReduction` :1816-1818, `ProdReduction` :1827-1831) inherit one generic trait at two instantiations, with the library's own comment calling it *"Hack to permit any Number to work non-parametrically"*, a shape the spec neither permits nor forbids and about which it carries an open editorial question (*"Does it include instantiations of parametric traits?"*, `traits.tex:167-171`); the remaining **21** are the comparison, numeric and `Maybe` towers, where the checker enforces consequences of `comprises` that the spec states nowhere. Which of the four clauses fires at which site was not traced: the clauses were read, the per-site attribution was not.

**C is the clean case and it is a library defect.** `RangeInternals.fsi` declares four traits requiring `[\I extends Integral[\I\]\]` (`:44, :121, :235, :304`) and then instantiates them from declarations whose own parameter is unbounded (`object RightScalarRange[\I\]` at `:309`, `emptyScalarRange[\I\]()` at `:578`) or bounded only by the non-parametric `AnyIntegral` (`sized1Range[\I extends AnyIntegral\]` at `:580`, and nine more). The interpreter checks no static-parameter bound, so nothing ever reported them. D is the same kind of thing: `trait String` declares `splitWithOffsets()` and `split()` twice, once `abstract` at `:2311-2312` and once concrete at `:2327-2328`. F is a real covariance violation across two files: `List[\E\].zip` returns `Generator[\(E,F)\]` (`List.fsi:99`) where the `ZeroIndexed[\E\].zip` it overrides returns `ZeroIndexed[\(E,F)\]` (`FortressLibrary.fsi:1187`).

**The checker gap is not in this list.** It is the crash that follows it: `nat`, `int`, `bool`, `dim` and `unit` static parameters are unimplemented in the checker (`STypesUtil.scala:546-559`), and the interpreter's library carries 81 declarations that use them. That is a separate, already-planned step (`reviews/nat-checking-plan.md`, PLAN step 4) and it blocks routes (b) and (c) equally.

## 4. The three routes, costed

Units. A **rung** is one declaration plus its failing test under the full gate; the eight-rung climb of 2026-09-17 took 8h37m, median 54 minutes a rung (`iteration-cost.md` §A). A **gated batch** is up to four rungs under one gate, measured saving 58.2 minutes over eight (`batched-climb-plan.md` §9). A **worker session** is one delegated report with its probe, of which this is one.

**(a) Keep growing the compiler world's prelude — the standard library written twice.** Costed by what it has already done: eight rungs moved the compile-path pass count from 59 to 81 of 410 corpus files, +22 (`compile-ladder/CLIMB.md:44-50`), and thirteen revival commits grew the four compiler-prelude files by 298 lines. The next fourteen fork-free rungs are forecast to move 38 files, mostly by one phase and not to a pass (`next-climb.md` §0). *Blocks:* nothing; it is the only route that can proceed today without a decision. *Forecloses:* nothing technically, but 104 of the 303 non-passing `tests/` files sit behind the array representation, `nat` parameters or the generator tower, and none of those is reachable by a rung — so the route runs out before the target program, and every declaration it writes is the copy the other two routes would delete.

**(b) One library, the interpreter's, made to pass the checker.** Three pieces in this order (`perf-probes/prelude/REPORT.md` §5). First `nat` kinds in the checker: PLAN step 4, five Scala/Java files plus an optional AST node, with a shadow-prototype recipe and a five-clause gate already written (`reviews/nat-checking-plan.md` §e, §f) — larger than a batch, smaller than a climb. Second the 93 errors at 48 sites: C, D and F (18 sites) are ordinary library edits, a batch or two; A, B and E (27 sites, the two E sites being among them) are not edits but a language-design conversation about `comprises` and exclusion, to be settled against the spec first — one worker session to state the question with the spec text and the four checker clauses beside it, then edits. Third the natives: about 79 of the 108 `builtinPrimitive` bindings in `FortressLibrary.fss` already have a `nativeHelpers/` counterpart under another name, about 29 do not, and the interpreter's remaining 319 bindings live in files the compiler world does not load. *Blocks:* every compiler-prelude rung written in the meantime becomes work to discard. *Forecloses:* the compiler world's own spellings where they differ — `NothingObject[\T\]`/`Nothing` against `Nothing[\T\]`, `Character` against `Char`, `Option`/`Some`/`NoneObject` against `Maybe`/`Just` (`array-design-review.md` §3c). *Does not settle:* whether the code generator can compile it. No run has ever reached DESUGAR or CODEGEN with this library.

**(c) One text, two native bindings.** The layer written once in `Library/`, with the native binding the only per-world file (`array-design-review.md` §3, decision C3, which records it as unprobed). *What is now known that was not:* the compiler's binding mechanism is wired on the interpreter's side too (§2), and no interpreter test exercises it, so the first experiment is one probe — a two-declaration component bound with `import java`, run under `fortress <file>.fss` — at roughly half a worker session. *What it still costs if that probe is green:* the same 93 errors and the same `nat` gap as (b), because a shared text meets the same checker; plus the three desugaring settings (`Shell.java:371-386`) reconciled and the four well-known types that the two worlds place in different apis (`Types.java:72-83`). *Forecloses:* the compiler world as a place to try a declaration the interpreter must not see — every rung of the last climb relied on exactly that (`next-climb/worlds.md`: an edit confined to `CompilerLibrary`/`CompilerBuiltin` cannot affect the 382 interpreter tests, with two named exceptions).

**Where the team's breadcrumbs point, and where they stop.** They point at the split being provisional, in their own words: *"hopefully temporary hack"* in a comment written the day it was made and still in the tree (`WellKnownNames.java:109-111`), *"stripped-down minimalist … for first crack at compilation"* in the birth commit (`c8d301411`), *"bogus"* in 2009 and *"bogo-trait"* in 2012 for what went into it, and a specification that recognizes one default library and never names the compiler's. They do **not** point at any of the three routes. Nothing on record says how the split was meant to end, or that it was meant to end at all; the last month of the project was spent adding to the compiler prelude. "Temporary" is evidence about intent, not about method: it is equally consistent with (b) and with (c), and it is not evidence against (a), which is what the team in fact did for three and a half years. The one thing the evidence does settle is negative and useful: the obstacle is not bytecode generation. 95.3% of `FortressLibrary.fss` is plain Fortress, and none of it has ever reached the desugarer or the code generator, because the checker stops it first.

# The library route: judgement

Terms. **Prelude**: the apis every program gets without importing them. **World**: a prelude plus its switches (`Shell.useCompilerLibraries()`); `fortress file.fss` runs the interpreter's world, `fortress compile` the compiler's. **Checker**: the static type checker, which runs only in the compiler's world. **Builtins**: the prelude's lowest layer, where declarations are bound to Java code (**natives**). **Exclusion**: the rule that two types share no value, which lets the checker refuse a trait extending both. **`nat`**: a static parameter that is a number, used for array sizes. **Rung**: one edit plus its test under the full gate (median 54 minutes). **Gated batch**: up to four rungs under one gate (3 to 5 hours landed). **Worker session**: one delegated report with its probe, no gate.

## 1. Is there a reason on record to keep a second library?

No. Nothing on record argues for two libraries as a destination, and Pavol's reading is the record's: the split was made on 2008-12-19 as a "stripped-down minimalist … first crack at compilation"; its switch is commented "hopefully temporary hack" in the tree today (`WellKnownNames.java:109-111`); the team called what went into it "bogus" (2009) and "bogo-trait" (June 2012, its last edit); the specification names one default library and never the compiler's (`library/structure.tex:13-22`, `default-libraries.tex:15-24`; no `.tex` in the tree contains the word `CompilerLibrary`). What the team did not leave is a plan for ending it: they grew the copy for three and a half years behind the wall they named at the wind-down, the type system against the JVM. That is a record of what they could do, not a position; overruling it costs nothing.

Each reason the brief and the reviews raise, judged:

- **A place the interpreter cannot see.** True (`next-climb/worlds.md`: an edit confined to the compiler prelude cannot reach the 384 interpreter tests) and never used: every batch gate has run `testSystem` anyway (`climb-batch-workflow.md:44`). Under one library a library edit is checked by both suites, which is the discipline Pavol set, not a loss. Not a reason for two.
- **Two native mechanisms.** Real, and a reason for two *binding* files, not two libraries: 95.3% of `FortressLibrary.fss` is plain Fortress; the natives are 108 bindings there and 231 in `FortressBuiltin.fss`, the builtins layer the specification itself separates from the library. Work before: re-bind those 339 (79 of the 108 have a `nativeHelpers` counterpart; the 231's overlap is uncounted, though the compiler's 330 `import java` aliases cover the same types). Whether the builtins are one text with `import java` on both paths, or one api with a component per path, is decided by a half-session probe nobody has run: `ForeignJava` is wired into the interpreter at `Driver.java:441` and exercised by no test. Not a reason for two.
- **The desugaring settings and the four well-known types.** One setting differs in substance: the compiler world gives an unbounded type parameter an implicit `extends Object`, and the specification says exactly that (`trait-parameters.tex:49-50`), so the compiler's setting is the spec's and the interpreter's is the divergence; the reconciliation keeps the compiler's. The four types (`String`, `JavaString`, `Exception`, `CheckedException`) are placed by `Types.useFortressLibraries()` once the world is one; the cost is the sources that name `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.X` literally (38 Java/Scala files, 21 of them the runtime's value classes such as `FZZ32`, plus the frozen stub `src/fortress/CompilerBuiltin.java`), a rename in the switch-over batch. Not a reason for two.
- **The checker's `nat` gap.** Blocks every route equally, growing the copy included, because the target vocabulary is sized (ruling of 2026-09-19). It is PLAN step 4 under any library. Not a reason for two.
- **The 27 exclusion sites.** The brief says only the `excludes` clause is in the specification. That is not right. The types chapter states three of the checker's four clauses: the `excludes` clause (`types-vals-vars.tex:212-214`), object-ness ("an object trait type excludes any type that is not its supertype", `:222-224`) and propagation to subtypes (`:163-164`). It does not state exclusion derived from `comprises`, and it contradicts the fourth clause: a trait "is allowed to extend other instantiations of itself" (`trait-parameters.tex:339-345`), while the checker's `checkP` (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:443-457`) makes two instantiations of one generic exclude each other, which is the shape of the numeric tower (`ZZ32 extends ZZ64`, both `Integral[\·\]`) and of the two reductions the library itself comments as a "Hack". Which clause fires at which of the 23 remaining sites was not traced. So this is work before: trace the clause per site (one worker session), then fix the library where a stated rule fires and the checker where the contradicted one does; a decision reaches Pavol only where the spec is silent, the `comprises` clause. The compiler world avoids this today only by keeping its tower flat (`ZZ32 extends { Number, Equality, StandardTotalOrder }`, no `ZZ64`, no `Integral`), the bogo-trait; a copy grown "in the library's own patterns" would meet the same rules. Not a reason for two.

One thing only one library gives: the checker on interpreter programs, which Pavol asked for on 2026-09-15 and which FACTS says means giving the checker the interpreter's prelude. It arrives the day the prelude passes TYPECHECK, before any native is ported.

## 2. The order

Destination: the compiler's prelude is the specification's, `AnyType`, `FortressBuiltin`, `FortressLibrary`, and `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin`, `CompilerAlgebra` are deleted at the switch-over. From `main` at the batch-2 landing:

**Step 0, now: stop adding to the compiler prelude.** Nothing is in flight (the tree is clean; the nine `wip/` remotes are landed batches awaiting deletion). The fourteen fork-free rungs were forecast to move 38 files by one phase and no microGPT component, and every one is a declaration `FortressLibrary` already has. Codegen rungs continue, being compiler work under any library: `forTryAtomicExpr` (row 353), `LetFn` (row 304), `ObjectExpr`, the eleven-file array-literal crash at `Misc.scala:876`. Prelude rungs (`Char`, `Thread`, `round`/`truncate`, `IndexOutOfBounds`) stop. The landed rungs' tests stay; the ten `library_tests` files that use compiler-world spellings (`NothingObject`, `Character`, `ZZ32Vector`) are rewritten at step 5.

**Step 1, the first rung: the interpreter prelude through the checker, as a gate stage.** Edit: `fortress typecheck` gets a `-fortress-lib` switch, the mirror of `-compiler-lib` (`Shell.java:860-863`; `typecheck` calls `useCompilerLibraries()` unconditionally today), or the 46-line `perf-probes/prelude/WorldFlip.java` moves into the harness; a stage in `climb-batch-workflow.js` beside the ladder regression runs the checker over the three apis and what they import under a private cache, prints the per-api error table and the crash line, and lands the table as the comparand. What it proves: that the distance to one library is measured by every gate from now on, and that the world switch is four lines. Stop condition: two runs print the same table (93 errors, 48 sites, 12 apis, `Not yet implemented` at `STypesUtil.scala:557`); the count is red, the suite is green; no library line changes. This is the one place the test-first rule is met by a stage rather than a `.fss`, because no program can yet be compiled against that prelude; the stage is permanent, which is what the rule protects.

Same batch, rungs 2 and 3, the defects with no question attached: family C, the fifteen `RangeInternals.fsi` bounds (`I extends AnyIntegral` where `Integral[\I\]` is required), 26 errors; families D and F and the site that extends and excludes `Condition[\()\]` in one line (`FortressLibrary.fsi:2526`), 4 errors. Gated by `testSystem`, which runs this code. Expected: 93 → 63 at 23 sites, nothing new. Stop: a fix that would change a declared type rather than a bound.

**Step 2, three worker sessions in parallel, no gate.** (a) The exclusion trace: for each of the 23 sites, which of the four clauses fires, beside the spec lines above; output: the sites under a stated rule (library rungs), the sites under the contradicted clause (a checker rung), and the sites under the `comprises` clause, the only decision that reaches Pavol. (b) The `nat` shadow session the review's decision F specifies: where the crash is (Scala or Java, finding 6), the export checker on the six dead-nat declarations (decision E: E2 in the checker, E3 the six-line api diff shown to Pavol), `NatExtends1`, `NatStore1`, and the loader probe that decides decision A (A2, the team's direction, against A3). (c) The half-session probe: a two-declaration component bound with `import java`, run by the interpreter; decides the builtins' shape for step 5.

**Step 3, the `nat` rung, then the exclusion rungs.** PLAN step 4 in the tree, shadow-proven, `.scala` plus whatever `.java` the shadow found: one to two gated batches. Decision E lands inside it. Then step 2(a)'s rungs, zero to two, or the `comprises` decision first. Stop condition of the phase: the stage prints zero errors and no crash, and `FlatArrays.fsi` type-checks with no error of its own (already true but for `nat`, FACTS). Milestone: `fortress typecheck -fortress-lib` works on interpreter programs.

**Step 4, one worker session: the prelude through DESUGAR and CODEGEN once.** No run has ever reached them with this library; the size is not on record. Output: the hole list, each hole a codegen rung, most of them rungs the ladder needs anyway.

**Step 5, the switch-over: at least two gated batches, with the one-`.java`-rung rule relaxed for them (as B1 proposed for the interpreter batch).** Batch one, the natives, re-bound as 2(c) decided: the 29 of 108 without a helper written, the 231 of `FortressBuiltin` matched to the compiler's helpers. Batch two, the names: the 38 sources and the frozen stub re-pointed; the two `useCompilerLibraries()` collapsed to one world with the extends-`Object` setting kept; the compile recipe's five files made three; the five prelude files deleted; the at least 48 compiler-side tests that name compiler-world spellings (a rough grep) rewritten to the spec's (`Nothing[\T\]`, `Char`). Gate: the full suite, the atomic runs, and the ladder regression, where the 85 passes must hold and the 104 fork-blocked files are expected to move off `Array is undefined`. Not settled: whether `FZZ32` implements `FortressLibrary.ZZ32` or `FortressBuiltin.Int` (the interpreter's `Int` is a value object under the trait; the compiler's value class is the trait's implementation); and, if 2(c) says two components, the mechanism, which is the step row 320 found missing (`Linker.whoIsImplementingMyAPI`).

**Step 6, decision D: a diff, no code.** The model's static types (D1 with D3, the review's default) shown to Pavol as the diff of `rmsn` and `step`'s signature, as soon as step 3 lands and before any array rung.

**Step 7, the array rungs against the library's existing `Array`, `Vector`, `Matrix`, with no copy to write.** Decision A's `.java` rungs as 2(b) decided, at least three gated batches (finding 6: `IntArg` in `extends` at `CodeGen.java:5784`, a runtime kind for `nat` arguments, the store); then decision B, unboxing by static type in generated code (B2), the largest codegen work in the plan, its first measurement `kdot` compiled over the store against `KDotPrim`. End state: the 31 declarations of `FlatArrays.fsi` type-check and compile against the one library, the model's text as D decided.

## 3. Costs, and what each route forecloses

| step | units |
|---|---|
| 1 | 1 gated batch (3 rungs) |
| 2 | 2 worker sessions + 1 half session |
| 3 | 1–2 gated batches + 0–2 rungs, or 1 decision first |
| 4 | 1 worker session + codegen rungs, count unknown |
| 5 | ≥ 2 gated batches |
| 6 | one diff |
| 7 | ≥ 3 gated batches, then B, unmeasured |

To the point where the prelude is one and the checker passes it: about four to five gated batches and four worker sessions. The array work after it is the same under any route.

Growing the copy to the same target costs the copy itself, the array layer and the algebra above `Number` written a second time (about 1,200 lines plus `AdditiveGroup`, `MultiplicativeRing`, `Indexed`, `ReadableArray`, finding 3), at least three batches; plus the same `nat` rung, the same A and B, the same exclusion rules as its tower grows; and never the checker on interpreter programs. It is cheaper only for the 38 files it can move by one phase.

Forecloses. One library: the compiler world's spellings (`NothingObject`, `Character`, `Option`/`Some`), which the goal already rules against; the never-used sandbox; the 298 lines of revival prelude text, superseded, their tests kept. Two libraries: the checker on interpreter programs; the array vocabulary without a copy; the standard library ever being one thing.

Not settled by the evidence, in the order it is met: whether `import java` runs under the interpreter (2c); which clause fires at each tower site (2a); whether the `nat` crash is in Scala or Java (2b); whether the loader can select a representation (2b); what the library meets in DESUGAR and CODEGEN (4); the overlap of the 231 builtins with the compiler's helpers (5); the size of B (7).

## 4. The decision

What we do: make the specification's default library, `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`, the compiler's prelude, and delete `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` and `CompilerAlgebra` when the switch-over lands; from now on no declaration goes into the compiler prelude, and codegen rungs continue.

What it changes: the standard library exists once; every library edit is gated by both suites; the checker becomes usable on interpreter programs when the prelude passes it; the array vocabulary is not written a second time; the thirteen revival commits to the compiler prelude are superseded and their tests kept.

Alternatives: keep growing the copy (reaches no microGPT component, runs out at 38 files, every line a copy to delete later); one text with two binding components for the builtins (a variant of the same destination, chosen by the step 2(c) probe, not by Pavol); both at once (two gates, no gain).

Default: one library, the interpreter's, with the builtins' shape decided by the probe. First rung: the interpreter prelude through the checker as a gate stage (step 1).

179:Where microGPT's 26 operations go is not a question after the third ruling: into `CompilerLibrary` in the library's own style, whose precedent for scalar extension is the `ZZ32` block at `FortressLibrary.fss:4477-4517` (`opr +(x: Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\], y: ZZ32)` beside `AdditiveGroup.+`, the same overloading shape the review found illegal by the letter and the interpreter accepts), for maps `map(f)` over `replica`, for structure the view objects, and for products the shared-nat operators of §6c.
163:Default: none can be labelled; this is the reserved fork and it is Pavol's. The cheapest fact before deciding is the classification of the 92 errors.
54:**(a) Keep growing the compiler world's prelude — the standard library written twice.** Costed by what it has already done: eight rungs moved the compile-path pass count from 59 to 81 of 410 corpus files, +22 (`compile-ladder/CLIMB.md:44-50`), and thirteen revival commits grew the four compiler-prelude files by 298 lines. The next fourteen fork-free rungs are forecast to move 38 files, mostly by one phase and not to a pass (`next-climb.md` §0). *Blocks:* nothing; it is the only route that can proceed today without a decision. *Forecloses:* nothing technically, but 104 of the 303 non-passing `tests/` files sit behind the array representation, `nat` parameters or the generator tower, and none of those is reachable by a rung — so the route runs out before the target program, and every declaration it writes is the copy the other two routes would delete.
65:What we do: make the specification's default library, `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`, the compiler's prelude, and delete `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` and `CompilerAlgebra` when the switch-over lands; from now on no declaration goes into the compiler prelude, and codegen rungs continue.
57:Growing the copy to the same target costs the copy itself, the array layer and the algebra above `Number` written a second time (about 1,200 lines plus `AdditiveGroup`, `MultiplicativeRing`, `Indexed`, `ReadableArray`, finding 3), at least three batches; plus the same `nat` rung, the same A and B, the same exclusion rules as its tower grows; and never the checker on interpreter programs. It is cheaper only for the 38 files it can move by one phase.
7:**What it is for.** Three small additions to the compiler's library, run through the batch machinery that ran batch 1, while the array design is written beside it as its own job. The array design is the real path to microGPT; this batch is what can be done without waiting for it, and it must not get in its way.
